 Steel Industry Pushes For 5% GST Rate To Address MSMEs' Working Capital Challenges
 By 
 siliconindia   |  Friday, 30 October 2026, 10:58:07 AM IST 
 Industry representatives are urging the government to reduce GST on steel to 5% to ease working capital pressures on micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). They argue that lower tax rates could reduce input costs, improve cash flows, support manufacturing competitiveness, and help smaller businesses manage rising operational expenses. 
 Industry representatives in Ludhiana are urging the government to reduce the Goods and Services Tax (GST) on steel from 18% to 5%, arguing that the existing tax structure is creating a significant working capital burden for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). The Federation of Industrial and Commercial Organization (FICO) says the inverted duty structure is affecting manufacturers across several engineering segments, including bicycles, sewing machines, agricultural equipment, and tractor components.
 FICO President Gurmeet Singh Kular has called for the tax reduction, stating that steel serves as a critical raw material for these industries, while several finished products attract a lower GST rate of 5%. This difference between input and output tax rates creates an accumulation of input tax credit (ITC), leaving manufacturers with substantial funds tied up in pending GST refunds instead of available cash for daily operations.
 Kular recently met National Traders Welfare Board Chairman Sunil Singhi and submitted a memorandum seeking a reduction in the GST rate on steel. He highlighted the financial pressure on manufacturers, noting that pending GST refunds in several cases exceed the bank credit limits available to industrial businesses. The delay forces companies to rely more heavily on external financing to meet production expenses, supplier payments, and other operational commitments.

 According to FICO, the current tax structure creates a liquidity mismatch for manufacturers that operate on relatively thin margins. Although businesses accumulate input tax credits because they pay higher taxes on raw materials than they collect on finished goods, delays in processing refunds prevent them from deploying that capital efficiently. Manufacturers estimate that nearly 13% of their working capital remains locked with the government for months, increasing their dependence on bank borrowing and raising financing costs.
 The industry body has also pointed to the government's decision to reduce GST on thread, an important raw material for the textile industry, as a precedent for addressing inverted duty structures through targeted tax rationalization. FICO argues that a similar reduction for steel could ease cost pressures across engineering and manufacturing supply chains while improving the competitiveness of domestic producers.
 Bicycle manufacturer Rakesh Aggarwal said manufacturers continue to face difficulties because their money remains tied up in government refunds even as they meet regular business expenses and loan repayment obligations. For smaller manufacturing units, prolonged cash-flow constraints can disrupt procurement cycles, delay production, and limit their ability to accept new orders.
 FICO maintains that GST rationalization is essential to improving the operating environment for MSMEs. A reduction in steel taxation could lower the upfront tax burden, release working capital, and reduce dependence on short-term credit. The government's response will be important for engineering manufacturers seeking greater financial flexibility and improved cost competitiveness.
